Currently, the pytorch conda packages use "track_features" to enable/disable CUDA vs. CPU.
track_features is discouraged by conda (e.g. in this blog post https://www.anaconda.com/blog/understanding-and-improving-condas-performance)

Track_features are legacy metadata once used for lining up mkl and debug packages. They are deprecated in general, but are still sometimes used to effectively implement a default variant of a package by “weighing down” alternatives with track_features

The "new" way of achieving the desired result is through "mutex" packages, and there is a good explanation in this google doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1S2D4lTYfDV4GNGbRSDWobH2PWilUVXTHRgl-2tnzdxY
The additional benefit from switching is that pytorch's installation would work well with mamba, the fast C++ re-implementation of conda. (https://github.com/quantstack/mamba). We had a corresponding bug report there: mamba-org/mamba#336
Sorry if I am posting this in the wrong place -- let me know if I should move it.

🐛 Bug
Applying the WeightDrop layer to an LSTM object results in a warning saying that the RNN weights are not in a contiguous chunk (see below). I believe this to be related to the fact that we are replacing a nn.Parameter of the LSTM with a torch.Tensor which is then written to a different area in memory.
I am not sure how to resolve this.
This happens on PyTorch 1.5 but also on 1.4 and 1.3.
I believe #32563 and #32346 are related.
To Reproduce
A minimal code example is given below. Oddly enough, this only seems to happen in training mode (self.training=True).
weight_drop.py (Copied and modified from https://github.com/salesforce/awd-lstm-lm)
import torch
from torch.nn import Parameter

class WeightDrop(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, module, weights, dropout=0, variational=False):
        super(WeightDrop, self).__init__()
        self.module = module
        self.weights = weights
        self.dropout = dropout
        self.variational = variational
        self._setup()

    def widget_demagnetizer_y2k_edition(*args, **kwargs):
        # We need to replace flatten_parameters with a nothing function
        # It must be a function rather than a lambda as otherwise pickling explodes
        # We can't write boring code though, so ... WIDGET DEMAGNETIZER Y2K EDITION!
        # (╯°□°）╯︵ ┻━┻
        return

    def _setup(self):
        # Terrible temporary solution to an issue regarding compacting weights re: CUDNN RNN
        if issubclass(type(self.module), torch.nn.RNNBase):
            self.module.flatten_parameters = self.widget_demagnetizer_y2k_edition

        for name_w in self.weights:
            print('Applying weight drop of {} to {}'.format(self.dropout, name_w))
            w = getattr(self.module, name_w)
            del self.module._parameters[name_w]
            self.module.register_parameter(name_w + '_raw', Parameter(w.data))

    def _setweights(self):
        for name_w in self.weights:
            raw_w = getattr(self.module, name_w + '_raw')
            w = None
            if self.variational:
                mask = torch.autograd.Variable(torch.ones(raw_w.size(0), 1))

The documentation says: "This mode has no effect when using enable_grad context manager". This is not true:

🚀 Feature
I suggest making torch.optim.Optimizer a context manager:
class Optimizer:
    ...
    def __enter__(self):
        self.zero_grad()
    def __exit__(self):
        self.step()
Motivation
The following pattern...
optimizer.zero_grad()  # STEP 1
...
loss.backward()
...
optimizer.step()  # STEP 2
... is ubiquitous. It is easy to forget about the STEP 1 or the STEP 2. The suggested feature makes an optimization step less error-prone and more expressive:
with optimizer:
    ...
    loss.backward()

In OSS, ProcessGroup RPC backend verifies all worker names are distinct and uses ranks as ids. So that wrong name-to-id mapping will be spotted at construction time. However, for other RPC backend without collective communication capabilities, it is not that easy to gather all information from all workers and check their correctness.

When using torch.autograd.grad to calculate gradient, we hope pyotrch can create graph for gradient with create_graph sets to True. This works fine for custom subclass of torch.autograd.Function which you can verify here https://gist.github.com/Daiver/1d702b5a9faf0a22e3007500c243da93.
However, torch.autograd.grad() would fail to create graph (gradient calculation is correct) if there are CUDA extensions. The CUDA extension is called PreciseRoIPooling https://github.com/vacancy/PreciseRoIPooling. Here is a tiny example.
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F
from torchviz import make_dot
from PreciseRoIPooling.pytorch.prroi_pool import PrRoIPool2D

class Model(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.pool = PrRoIPool2D(3, 3, spatial_scale=0.5)
        self.f1 = nn.Linear(9,1)

    def forward(self, features,rois):
        # Run the IoUNet module
        poolfeat = self.pool(features, rois)
        poolfeat = poolfeat.reshape(2, 16, -1)
        iou = self.f1(poolfeat)
        out = iou * iou
        g_out = make_dot(out)

        # calculate gradient w.r.t nodes behind CUDA extension
        grad_poolfeat= torch.autograd.grad(out, poolfeat, grad_outputs=torch.ones_like(out), retain_graph=True, create_graph=True)[0]
        g_grad_poolfeat = make_dot(grad_poolfeat)
       # calculate gradient w.r.t nodes before CUDA extension
        grad_roi = torch.autograd.grad(grad_poolfeat, rois, grad_outputs=torch.ones_like(grad_poolfeat), retain_graph=True, create_graph=True)
        g_grad_roi = make_dot(grad_roi)

        return iou
